section.heading: 10.1. Probability Distributions of Random Variables
Probability
section.paragraph: We begin by discussing some terminology and notation that are important in the study of probability.

note.source_type: Experiment, Outcome, Sample Point, Sample Space, and Event
note.title: Experiment, Outcome, Sample Point, Sample Space, and Event
note.heading: Experiment, Outcome, Sample Point, Sample Space, and Event
note.paragraph: An experiment is an activity with observable results called outcomes , or sample points . The totality of all outcomes is the sample space of the experiment. A subset of the sample space is called an event of the experiment.

section.paragraph: Now, given an event associated with an experiment, our primary objective is to determine the likelihood that this event will occur. This likelihood, or probability of the event , is a number between $$0$$ and $$1$$ and may be viewed as the proportionate number of times that the event will occur if the experiment associated with the event is repeated indefinitely under independent and similar conditions. Consider the simple experiment of tossing an unbiased coin and observing whether it lands “heads” $$(H)$$ or “tails” $$(T)$$ . Since the coin is unbiased, we see that the probability of each outcome is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ , abbreviated
and
section.heading: Discrete Random Variables
section.paragraph: We often assign numerical values to the outcomes of an experiment. For example, suppose an experiment consists of throwing a die and observing the face that lands up. If we let $$X$$ denote the outcome of the experiment, then $$X$$ assumes one of the values $$1$$ , $$2$$ , $$3$$ , $$4$$ , $$5$$ , or $$6$$ . Because the values assumed by $$X$$ depend on the outcomes of a chance experiment, the outcome $$X$$ is referred to as a random variable . In this case, the random variable $$X$$ is also said to be finite discrete, since it can assume only a finite number of integer values.

The function $$P$$ that associates with each value of a random variable its probability of occurrence is called a probability function. It is discrete because its domain consists of a finite set. In general, a discrete probability function is defined as follows.

note.title: Discrete Probability Function
note.heading: Discrete Probability Function
note.paragraph: A discrete probability function $$P$$ with domain $$\left\{ x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} \right\}$$ satisfies these conditions:

list.item: $$0 \leq P\left( x_{i} \right) \leq 1$$ , for $$1 \leq i \leq n$$
$$P\left( x_{1} \right) + P\left( x_{2} \right) + \cdots + P\left( x_{n} \right) = 1$$

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: These conditions state that the probability assigned to an outcome must be nonnegative and less than or equal to $$1$$ and that the sum of all probabilities must be $$1$$ .

section.heading: Histograms
section.paragraph: We can exhibit a discrete probability function or probability distribution graphically by constructing a histogram . First locate the values of the random variable on a horizontal line. Then, above each number, erect a rectangle whose height is equal to the probability associated with that value of the random variable.

For example, consider the data in Table 1, the number of cars observed waiting in line at $$2$$ -minute intervals between 3 p.m. and 5 p.m. on a certain Friday at the drive-in teller of the Westwood Savings Bank and the corresponding frequency of occurrence. If we divide each number on the right of the table by $$60$$ (the sum of these numbers), then we obtain the respective probabilities associated with the random variable $$X$$ , when $$X$$ assumes the values $$0,1,2,\ldots,8$$ . For example,
$$\begin{array}{ccl} {P\left( {X = 0} \right)} & = & {\frac{2}{60} \approx .03} \\ {P\left( {X = 1} \right)} & = & {\frac{9}{60} = .15} \\ { \vdots} & & \end{array}$$
The resulting probability distribution is shown in Table 2.

Observe that the area of a rectangle in a histogram is associated with a value of a random variable $$X$$ and that this area gives precisely the probability associated with that value of $$X$$ . This follows because each rectangle, by construction, has width $$1$$ and height corresponding to the probability associated with the value of the random variable.

section.paragraph: Another consequence arising from the method of construction of a histogram is that the probability associated with more than one value of the random variable $$X$$ is given by the sum of the areas of the rectangles associated with those values of $$X$$ . For example, the probability that three or four cars are in line is given by
$$P\left( {X = 3} \right) + P\left( {X = 4} \right)$$
which may be obtained from the histogram by adding the areas of the rectangles associated with the values $$3$$ and $$4$$ of the random variable $$X$$ . Thus, the required probability is
$$P\left( {X = 3} \right) + P\left( {X = 4} \right) = .20 + .13 = .33$$
section.heading: Continuous Random Variables
section.paragraph: A random variable $$X$$ that can assume any value in an interval is called a continuous random variable . Examples of continuous random variables are the life span of a light bulb, the length of a telephone call, the length of an infant at birth, the daily amount of rainfall in Boston, and the life span of a certain plant species. For the remainder of this section, we are interested primarily in continuous random variables.

Consider an experiment in which the associated random variable $$X$$ has the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ as its sample space. Then an event of the experiment is any subset of $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . For example, if $$X$$ denotes the life span of a light bulb, then the sample space associated with the experiment is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ , and the event that a light bulb selected at random has a life span between $$500$$ and $$600$$ hours, inclusive, is described by the interval $$\left\lbrack {500,600} \right\rbrack$$ or, equivalently, by the inequality $$500 \leq X \leq 600$$ . The probability that the light bulb will have a life span of between $$500$$ and $$600$$ hours is denoted by $$P\left( {500 \leq X \leq 600} \right)$$ .

In general, we will be interested in computing $$P\left( {a \leq X \leq b} \right)$$ , the probability that a random variable $$X$$ assumes a value in the interval $$a \leq X \leq b$$ . This computation is based on the notion of a probability density function, which we now introduce.

note.title: Probability Density Function
note.heading: Probability Density Function
note.paragraph: A probability density function of a random variable $$X$$ in an interval $$I$$ , where $$I$$ may be bounded or unbounded, is a nonnegative function $$f$$ having the following properties.

list.item: The total area of the region under the graph of $$f$$ is equal to $$1$$ (Figure 2a).

The probability that an observed value of the random variable $$X$$ lies in the interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ is given by $$P(a \leq X \leq b) = {\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ (Figure 2b). Figure 2 Details There are two images a and b each graphed a bell shaped curve in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. In image a, the x and y axes are unmarked and unlabeled. The curve starts just above the x axis, a short distance away from the origin, slopes upward to the right, concave up, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes up, now concave down, and reaches the high point. From its high point, the curve goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches its inflection point, it goes down to the right, but concave up and ends very close to the x axis. The region below the curve is shaded and is labeled R. In image b, the x axis has marks labeled a and b, appear at unequal intervals. The curve starts just above the x axis, a short distance away from the origin, slopes upward to the right, concave up, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes up, now concave down, and reaches the high point. From its high point, the curve goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches its inflection point, it goes down to the right, but concave up and ends very close to the x axis. Two vertical lines rises from the marks a and b on the x axis, till it reaches the curve. The region bounded by the curve, x axis and the two vertical lines is shaded and the region is labeled P (a <= X <= b).
Property 1 states that the probability that a continuous random variable takes on a value lying in its range is $$1$$ , a certainty, which is expected.

Property 2 states that the probability that the random variable $$X$$ assumes a value in an interval $$a \leq X \leq b$$ is given by the area of the region between the graph of $$f$$ and the $$x$$ -axis from $$X = a$$ to $$X = b$$ . Because the area under one point on the graph of $$f$$ is equal to zero, we see that $$P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b) = P(a < X < b)$$ .

A probability density function of a random variable $$X$$ may be constructed by using methods that range from theoretical considerations of the problem on one extreme to an interpretation of data associated with the experiment on the other.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Show that each of the following functions satisfies the nonnegativity condition and Property 1 of probability density functions.

list.item: $$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x} (0 \leq x < \infty)$$

example.heading: Solution

list.item: Since the factors $$x$$ and $$(x - 1)$$ are both nonnegative on $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack$$ , we see that $$f(x) \geq 0$$ on $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack$$ . Next, we compute $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = {\frac{2}{27}{\int_{1}^{4}{({x^{2} - x})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = \left. \frac{2}{27}\left( {\frac{1}{3}x^{3} - \frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right) \right|_{1}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = \left. \frac{2}{27}\left\lbrack \left( {\frac{64}{3} - 8} \right) - \left( {\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{2}} \right) \right. \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = {\frac{2}{27}\left( \frac{27}{2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = 1} \end{array}$$ showing that Property 1 of probability density functions holds as well.

First, $$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x} \geq 0$$ for all values of $$x$$ in $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ . Next, $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{0}^{b}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = \left. \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty} - e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x} \right|_{0}^{b}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{({- e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}b} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = 1} \end{array}$$ so the area under the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x}$$ on $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ is equal to $$1$$ , as we set out to show.

If $$X$$ is a continuous random variable with the probability density function given in part (a), compute the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value between $$1$$ and $$2$$ .

note.title: Note
note.heading: Note
note.paragraph: Observe that the probability that a continuous random variable $$X$$ will assume a value at a number $$a$$ is zero, since $$P\left( {X = a} \right) = \int_{a}^{a}{f(x)dx = 0}$$ . (See Probability Density Function.)

note.title: Uniform Density Function
note.heading: Uniform Density Function
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be the constant probability density function
$$f(x) = \frac{1}{b - a} (a \leq x \leq b)$$
defined on an interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ , where $$a < b$$ . Then $$f$$ is called a uniform density function on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ .

section.paragraph: A random variable that has a uniform density function is said to be uniformly distributed. An application involving a uniform distribution follows.

note.title: Applied Example 4. Musical Fountains
note.heading: Applied Example 4. Musical Fountains
note.paragraph: “The Fountains of Bellagio” is a choreographed water display set to light and music that takes place in front of the Bellagio Hotel in Las Vegas. In the evening, the shows take place every $$15$$ minutes from 7 p.m. to midnight. The duration of each show is $$7$$ minutes. If Joan arrives at a random time between 7 p.m. and 7:15 p.m. for an evening show and finds the fountains not performing, find the probability that Joan will have to wait at least $$5$$ minutes before the next show starts.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Let $$X$$ denote the time (in minutes) that Joan has to wait for the next show. Then $$X$$ is uniformly distributed over the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,8} \right\rbrack$$ . (The fountains are not performing for a duration of $$8$$ minutes each time the show is not on.) So the uniform density function associated with this problem is
$$f(x) = \frac{1}{8} \left( {0 \leq x \leq 8} \right)$$
and the desired probability is
$$P\left( {5 \leq X \leq 8} \right) = {\int_{5}^{8}\frac{1}{8}}dx = \left. {\frac{1}{8}x} \right|_{5}^{8} = \frac{1}{8}\left( {8 - 5} \right) = \frac{3}{8}$$

note.source_type: Applied Example 5. Life Span of Light Bulbs
note.title: Applied Example 5. Life Span of Light Bulbs
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Life Span of Light Bulbs
note.paragraph: TKK Products manufactures a $$200$$ -watt electric light bulb. Laboratory tests show that the life spans of these light bulbs have a distribution described by the probability density function
Determine the probability that a light bulb will have a life span of

list.item: (a) $$500$$ hours or less,
(b) more than $$500$$ hours, and
(c) more than $$1000$$ hours but less than $$1500$$ hours.

note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Let $$X$$ denote the life span of a light bulb.

list.item: The probability that a light bulb will have a life span of $$500$$ hours or less is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(0 \leq X \leq 500)} = {\int_{0}^{500}{0.001e^{- 0.001x}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P(0 \leq X \leq 500)} = - {\left. e^{- 0.001x} \right|_{0}^{500} = - e^{- 0.5} + 1}} \\ {\phantom{P(0 \leq X \leq 500)} \approx 0.3935} \end{array}$$

The probability that a light bulb will have a life span of more than $$500$$ hours is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(X > 500)} = {\int_{500}^{\infty}{0.001e^{- 0.001x}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 500)} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{500}^{b}{0.001e^{- 0.001x}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 500)} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left. {- e^{- 0.001x}} \right|}_{500}^{b}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 500)} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}( - e^{- 0.001b} + e^{- 0.5})}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 500)} = {e^{- 0.5} \approx 0.6065}} \end{array}$$ This result may also be obtained by observing that $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(X > 500)} = {1 - P(X \leq 500)}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 500)} = {1 - 0.3935} {{Use the result from part}(a).}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 500)} \approx 0.6065} \end{array}$$

The probability that a light bulb will have a life span of more than $$1000$$ hours but less than $$1500$$ hours is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {1000 < X < 1500} \right)} = {\int_{1000}^{1500}{0.001e^{- 0.001x}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {1000 < X < 1500} \right)} = \left. {- e^{- 0.001x}} \right|_{1000}^{1500}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {1000 < X < 1500} \right)} = {- e^{- 1.5} + e^{- 1}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {1000 < X < 1500} \right)} \approx {- 0.2231 + 0.3679}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {1000 < X < 1500} \right)} = 0.1448} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: The probability density function of Example 5 is called an exponential density function . More generally, we have the following.

note.title: Exponential Density Function (with Parameter k )
note.heading: Exponential Density Function (with Parameter k )
note.paragraph: Let $$f$$ be the function defined by
$$f(x) = ke^{- kx} (0 \leq x < \infty)$$
where $$k$$ is a positive constant. Then $$f$$ is called an exponential density function with parameter $$k$$ on $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ .

section.paragraph: You are asked to verify that $$f$$ is a probability density function in Exercise 61. The graph of $$f$$ is shown in Figure 4. The random variable that is associated with $$f$$ is said to be exponentially distributed. Exponential random variables are used to represent the life span of an electronic component, the duration of a telephone call, the waiting time in a doctor’s office, and the time between successive flight arrivals and departures in an airport, to mention but a few applications.

section.heading: Joint Probability Density Functions
section.paragraph: Sometimes the outcomes of an experiment are associated with more than one random variable. For example, we might be interested in the relationship between the weight and height of newborn infants or between the price and tread life of automobile tires. To study such problems, we need to extend the concept of a probability density function of a random variable to functions of more than one variable. In the case involving two random variables, we have the following definition.

note.title: Joint Probability Density Function
note.heading: Joint Probability Density Function
note.paragraph: A joint probability density function of the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ on a region $$D$$ is a nonnegative function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ having the property
$$\iint\limits_{D}{f(x,y)dA = 1}$$
Thus, the volume of the solid under the graph of $$f$$ is equal to $$1$$ .
The probability that the observed values of the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ lie in a region $$R \subset D$$ is given by
$$P\left\lbrack {\left( {X,Y} \right){in}R} \right\rbrack = {\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA}}$$

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ be the joint probability density function for the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ on $$D = \left\{ \left. \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leq x \leq 1;0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\} \right.$$ . Find

list.item: (a) $$P{({0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2})}$$ and
(b) $$P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)$$ .

example.heading: Solution

list.item: The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1 \slash 2}{xydxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\left( \left. {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}y} \right|_{0}^{1 \slash 2} \right)dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{8}ydy = \left. {\frac{1}{16}y^{2}} \right|_{1}^{2} = \frac{3}{16}}}} \end{array}$$

The region $$R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x + y \leq 1 \right\}$$ is shown in Figure 5. The required probability is $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{1 - x}{xydydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( \left. {\frac{1}{2}xy^{2}} \right|_{0}^{1 - x} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{1}{2}x\left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({x - 2x^{2} + x^{3}})}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}\left. \left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{2} - \frac{2}{3}x^{3} + \frac{1}{4}x^{4}} \right) \right|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{4}} \right) = \frac{1}{24}}} \end{array}$$ Figure 5 Details A line x + y = 1 is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from 0 to beyond 1 and the y axis ranges from 0 to over 1. The line enters the second quadrant from the top, cuts the y axis at (0, 1), goes down to the right, cuts the x axis at (1, 0), and enters the fourth quadrant. The region below the line is shaded and the region is labeled R.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2e^{- x - 2y}$$ be the joint probability density function for the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ on $$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x \geq 0 \right.$$ and $$\left. y \geq 0 \right\}$$ .

list.item: Find the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value between $$0$$ and $$1$$ and that $$Y$$ will assume a value between $$1$$ and $$2$$ .
Find the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value greater than $$1$$ and that $$Y$$ will assume a value less than $$2$$ .

example.heading: Solution

list.item: The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{2e^{- x - 2y}dxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = \int_{1}^{2}\left( \left. - 2e^{- x - 2y} \right|_{0}^{1} \right)dy} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{{({- 2e^{- 1 - 2y} + 2e^{- 2y}})}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{2(1 - e^{- 1})e^{- 2y}dy}} {{Simplify the integrand}.}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {2(1 - e^{- 1})\left. \left( {- \frac{1}{2}e^{- 2y}} \right) \right|_{1}^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = \left. - (1 - e^{- 1})e^{- 2y} \right|_{1}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {- (1 - e^{- 1})(e^{- 4} - e^{- 2}) \approx .0740}} \end{array}$$

The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{1}^{\infty}{2e^{- x - 2y}dxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\left( {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{b}{2e^{- x - 2y}}}dx} \right)dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {{\int_{0}^{2}\left( \left. {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty} - 2e^{- x - 2y}} \right|_{1}^{b} \right)}dy}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\lbrack\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}( - 2e^{- b - 2y} + 2e^{- 1 - 2y})\rbrack dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {{\int_{0}^{2}{2e^{- 1 - 2y}}}dy}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\left. - e^{- 1 - 2y} \right|_{0}^{2} = - e^{- 5} + e^{- 1} \approx .3611}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Using Technology Graphing a Histogram
Graphing Utility
section.paragraph: A graphing utility can be used to plot the histogram for a given set of data, as illustrated in the following example.

note.title: Applied Example 1.
note.heading: Applied Example 1.
note.paragraph: A survey of $$90,000$$ households conducted in a certain year revealed the following percentage of women who wear a shoe size within the given ranges.

Let $$X$$ denote the random variable taking on the values $$1$$ through $$8$$ , where $$1$$ corresponds to a shoe size less than $$5$$ , $$2$$ corresponds to a shoe size of $$5-5\frac{1}{2}$$ , and so on.

list.item: Plot a histogram for the given data.
What percentage of women in the survey wear a shoe size within the ranges $$7-7\frac{1}{2}$$ or $$8-8\frac{1}{2}$$ ?

note.heading: Solution

list.item: Enter the values of $$X$$ as $$x_{1} = 1,x_{2} = 2,\ldots,x_{8} = 8$$ and the corresponding values of $$Y$$ as $$y_{1} = 1,y_{2} = 5,\ldots,y_{8} = 2$$ . Then using the draw function from the Statistics menu, we draw the histogram shown in Figure T1. Figure T1 Details The figure shows a histogram in the first quadrant of the viewing window. The horizontal axis ranges from 0 to 9 and the vertical axis ranges from 0 to 35. Above each number, a vertical rectangle of uniform width and different heights is raised on the horizontal axis, each adjoining the next, without any intervals. The width of each rectangle is 1 unit runs along the x axis. The width of the first rectangle runs from the mark 0.5 to 1.5 and it reaches to a height of 1 unit, the width of the second rectangle runs from 1.5 to 2.5 and it reaches to a height of 5 units, the width of the third rectangle runs from 2.5 to 3.5 and it reaches to a height of 15 units, the width of the fourth rectangle runs from 3.5 to 4.5 and it reaches to a height of 27 units, the width of the fifth rectangle runs from 4.5 to 5.5 and it reaches to a height of 29 units, the width of sixth rectangle runs from 5.5 to 6.5 one reaches to a height of 14 units, the width of seventh one runs from 6.5 to 7.5 and it reaches to a height of 7 units, and the width of eighth one runs from 7.5 to 8.5 and it reaches to a height of 2 units. The histogram for the given data, using the viewing window $$\left\lbrack {0,9} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {0,35} \right\rbrack$$

The probability that a woman participating in the survey wears a shoe size within the ranges $$7-7\frac{1}{2}$$ or $$8-8\frac{1}{2}$$ is given by $$P(X = 4) + P(X = 5) = .27 + .29 = .56$$ This tells us that $$56\%$$ of the women wear a shoe size within the ranges $$7-7\frac{1}{2}$$ or $$8-8\frac{1}{2}$$ .
